cards.power: Third-Person Gaslighting. Play to rewrite an opponent's successful turn as a catastrophic failure. They must accept your version of reality.
cards.lore: The general wrote a clean, readable memoir acting like a neutral observer of his own continental slaughter.
cards.gradeReason: You immediately become Caesar lying to your face about what just happened.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: ink wash satire. Subject: vulture in toga writing at a desk while carnage blazes behind him. Mood: serene self-congratulation.

cards.power: Geographic Pretext. Divide the game board into top, bottom, and middle. Opponent must not exist in each.
cards.lore: The most famous opening line in military memoir history is just a fancy way of saying 'I came to conquer all three.'
cards.gradeReason: 'Must not exist in each' reads garbled — unclear what player is actually doing.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: old Roman map parody. Subject: badger general pointing at a map divided into three sections. Mood: bureaucratic aggression.

cards.power: Institutional Math. Delete half the opponent's deck. Call it 'Pacification.'
cards.lore: Institutional assessments can treat corpses as logistics. The Gauls are treated as terrifying as the Romans need to justify the math.
cards.gradeReason: The euphemism IS the mechanic. You enact imperial violence and name it correctly.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: satirical ledger illustration. Subject: bureaucrat fox tallying bones on an abacus. Mood: cold administrative horror.

cards.power: Unwritten Memory. Hide three cards in your pocket. The opponent cannot forget what they cannot prove existed.
cards.lore: The specific institutional memory of the Celtic world was all written down. When the Romans burned the groves, they deleted the hard drive.
cards.gradeReason: Hiding cards IS the oral tradition — mechanic and concept fuse perfectly.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: mystical watercolor. Subject: owl clutching scrolls disappearing into pocket-shadows. Mood: knowing, ancient, unbothered.

cards.power: Strategic Defection. Switch alliances mid-game. Take all your current ally's resources with you.
cards.lore: Rome's primary client tribe learned the hard way that a Roman alliance has limits military pressure will eagerly expose.
cards.gradeReason: Clear betrayal card — works at table, lore explains the cost better than the power does.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: diplomatic satire. Subject: fox shaking two different hands simultaneously while pocketing coins. Mood: slick pragmatism.

cards.power: Demographic Avalanche. Move 380,000 tokens at once. Burn your base so you can't retreat.
cards.lore: A genuine demographic migration that Caesar intercepted, creating the perfect pretext for a war of total conquest.
cards.gradeReason: Strong concept but 'burn your base' is instruction, not invitation.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: chaotic migration cartoon. Subject: enormous badger herd flowing over a map, burning village behind them. Mood: unstoppable momentum.

cards.power: Displaced Pre-eminence. Gain +5 Attack if you are currently losing. The anger is on your side.
cards.lore: The wealthy plateau tribe whose status resentment over losing top-dog status made the pan-Gallic revolt its political urgency.
cards.gradeReason: 'The anger is on your side' — player immediately knows the emotional register to embody.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: wounded pride warrior illustration. Subject: stag standing taller in defeat, crown knocked sideways. Mood: defiant fury.

cards.power: Grassroots Sabotage. Disable the opponent's highest-value aristocratic card using mob rules.
cards.lore: The aristocrats loved the Roman patronage; the people knew it was just an elaborate leash.
cards.gradeReason: Good political satire — functional but the lore lands harder than the power text.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: protest cartoon. Subject: angry squirrel mob toppling a tall aristocratic fox. Mood: chaotic democratic energy.

cards.power: Barbarian Distance. Immune to 'Civilizing' effects. The further from the center you play them, the harder they hit.
cards.lore: Caesar called them the bravest because they were furthest from Mediterranean luxury and fought the Germans for fun.
cards.gradeReason: Strong spatial metaphor — needs 'Civilizing effects' defined in rules to fully unlock.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: wild frontier illustration. Subject: enormous wild boar charging from the edges of a map, snarling at center. Mood: peripheral ferocity.

cards.power: Camp Ambush. Attack while the opponent is still shuffling their deck.
cards.lore: They used terrain and timing to hit the Romans before formations could be completed, nearly ending Caesar's career in an afternoon.
cards.gradeReason: Clever timing mechanic — works well but stays mechanical rather than embodied.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: ambush moment watercolor. Subject: wolves erupting from forest edge at an unprepared army. Mood: sudden violent surprise.

cards.power: Fatal Trust. Convince an opponent to discard their hand to 'avoid a trap,' which is the actual trap.
cards.lore: The chieftain who earned a client's trust to bait fifteen Roman cohorts out of winter camp and straight into the meat grinder.
cards.gradeReason: Player immediately knows exactly what kind of person they're playing — the perfect betrayer.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: sinister hospitality illustration. Subject: smiling fox offering a hand in friendship while wolves wait behind trees. Mood: warm treachery.

cards.power: Mercenary Range. Play this card on any opponent's board. They fight for whoever pays the most attention.
cards.lore: The Gauls who went East. They had no druid tradition, not a reputation for ferocity that terrified Hellenistic kings into hiring them.
cards.gradeReason: Good mercenary flavor — 'pays the most attention' is sharp writing but mechanic needs table context.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: wandering warrior portrait. Subject: Gallic bear in mismatched armor standing at a crossroads map. Mood: for-hire professionalism.

cards.power: Tragic Sacrifice. Surrender this card to save your remaining deck. The opponent gets to gloat for 6 turns.
cards.lore: He built a genuinely pan-Gallic coalition, figured out the correct strategy, and lost because marginally better is enough for Rome.
cards.gradeReason: Surrendering the hero TO SAVE THE DECK — the mechanics ARE the tragedy.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: heroic sacrifice illustration. Subject: stag in chains lowering his antlers before a Roman eagle. Mood: noble devastating loss.

cards.power: Heavy Sword. When you score a throw, your sword on the scales. You win.
cards.lore: The Senonian chieftain who sacked Rome and summarized all asymmetric negotiation with five syllables: Vae Victis.
cards.gradeReason: Throw your weapon onto the table and win — you are Brennus, no explanation needed.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: triumphant brute illustration. Subject: bear throwing enormous sword onto a scale, scattering Roman coins. Mood: contemptuous supremacy.

cards.power: Mobile Skirmish. Never lock into combat. Deal damage and return this card to your hand immediately.
cards.lore: The British chieftain who refused to give the Romans the heavy infantry fight they wanted, opting to spend their day with chariots.
cards.gradeReason: Clear hit-and-run mechanic — works well but doesn't quite invite persona embodiment.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: chariot speed blur. Subject: hare on chariot striking and vanishing, Romans grasping at air. Mood: elusive defiance.

cards.power: Refusal to Cross. Cancel any forced-play effect. You die, but you don't have to.
cards.lore: The politician who understood Caesar was a permanent guest, not a guest, and was killed trying to escape the hostage tour.
cards.gradeReason: 'You die, but you don't have to' — five words that make this the most philosophically powerful card in the deck.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: defiant last stand. Subject: fox facing a Roman soldier with arms spread, refusing to board a ship. Mood: sovereign dignity in death.

cards.power: Divine Exemption. This card cannot be attacked. It directs all your other cards and makes the violence 'legitimate.'
cards.lore: They weren't just religious specialists; they were the command layer, the legal arbitrators, and the institutional memory.
cards.gradeReason: Strong institutional card — 'makes the violence legitimate' is a great line but the role needs context to perform.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: sacred authority illustration. Subject: robed owl directing battle from above while soldiers fight below. Mood: untouchable command.

cards.power: Theological Legitimation. Force an opponent to agree with your move because 'the gods (or the Senate) said so.'
cards.lore: The only Druid Caesar named. His cooperation was structurally necessary for the Roman client system to function in Gaul.
cards.gradeReason: Great political mechanic — the parenthetical '(or the Senate)' gets a laugh but lore outperforms the power.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: religious bureaucrat portrait. Subject: solemn owl in Roman toga making hand gestures at skeptical badgers. Mood: legitimate inevitability.

cards.power: Cedar-Oil Trophy. When you defeat an enemy card, pin it to your board. It generates four points every turn.
cards.lore: You don't sell your professional credentials. The head contains the soul; taking it transfers the enemy's power to the victor.
cards.gradeReason: Pinning defeated cards to your board — you ARE the head collector, the soul-transfer warrior.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: trophy wall horror-comedy. Subject: warrior fox proudly gesturing at a wall of pinned enemy cards. Mood: grim professional pride.

cards.power: Subterranean Memory. Long after your cards are destroyed, they still produce +1 Resource from the discard pile.
cards.lore: The pan-Gallic druidic council met here. Rome burned it and built a cathedral on top. But the spring remembers.
cards.gradeReason: Poetic mechanic — lore is perfect but '+1 Resource from discard pile' reads mechanically at the table.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: underground persistence watercolor. Subject: stone spring flowing beneath cathedral foundations at night. Mood: quiet ancient defiance.

cards.power: Survival Mathematics. Attack with zero defense. Your opponent takes psychological damage just watching you go.
cards.lore: They fought without armor as a deliberate ritual choice, communicating that normal survival mathematics did not apply to them.
cards.gradeReason: You attack naked and your opponent takes psychological damage. No explanation needed — you ARE the Gaesatae.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: terrifying body horror comedy. Subject: naked screaming badger charging at armored Romans who are visibly disturbed. Mood: unhinged transcendence.

cards.power: Acoustic Terror. Opponent must skip their next turn with their cards facing away from them.
cards.lore: The tall bronze trumpet with the animal head. Its harsh, discordant shriek was the specific signal that activated the Roman fear response.
cards.gradeReason: Making opponent turn their cards away from battle — player enacts the sonic panic. Pure table theater.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: battle cacophony illustration. Subject: enormous boar-headed bronze horn blasting sound waves at fleeing soldiers. Mood: auditory catastrophe.

cards.power: Honor Advertising. Place on a unit. If defeated, the opponent gets double points. If victorious, you get triple.
cards.lore: The twisted gold neck ring. Armor for the soul. A library of accumulated honor, and the ultimate trophy for a Roman looter.
cards.gradeReason: Honor-as-risk is great — double/triple point mechanic needs a moment of table explanation.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: sacred object illustration. Subject: glowing gold torc floating above a warrior's shoulders, shining dangerously bright. Mood: honor as temptation.

cards.power: Aristocratic Extraction. Save one of your defeated cards right before it dies by pulling it back to your hand.
cards.lore: Not an archery platform. A mobility tool for the elite warrior who fights on foot but needs the prestige of a drive-by arrival.
cards.gradeReason: Good rescue mechanic — 'prestige of a drive-by arrival' is the best lore line, power stays mechanical.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: aristocratic exit illustration. Subject: fox warrior leaping back onto chariot mid-battle, cape trailing. Mood: elite nonchalance.

cards.power: Open Melee. Devastating in open space, but loses power if the opponent clusters their cards together.
cards.lore: 90 centimeters of metallurgical superiority designed for slashing. Romans claimed they bent; archaeologists claim Romans lied.
cards.gradeReason: Spatial mechanic is solid — works well at the table but invites no particular persona.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: weapon portrait. Subject: enormous gleaming longsword with Gallic knotwork, mid-slash through open air. Mood: metallurgical pride.

cards.power: Socketed Impact. Pierce through an opponent's shield card and hit the unit behind it.
cards.lore: The heavy thrusting weapon that gave the naked Gaesatae their name. Big, iron, leaf-shaped, and terrifying.
cards.gradeReason: Shield-piercing is clear and satisfying — functional but not performative.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: impact illustration. Subject: leaf-bladed iron spear punching clean through a Roman shield. Mood: unstoppable momentum.

cards.power: Farmer's Reach. Can be equipped by any low-level card to instantly make them a ranged threat.
cards.lore: Everyone's weapon. The specific equipment the farming warrior carries from his fields to the battlefield and back.
cards.gradeReason: Good egalitarian card — 'Farmer's Reach' is a great name but the mechanic is utility, not theater.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: everyman warrior portrait. Subject: badger farmer holding a light spear, one hand still dirty from the field. Mood: democratic violence.

cards.power: Individual Block. Block an attack, but you cannot form a shield wall with other cards.
cards.lore: A personal tool for individual combat, unlike the Roman Scutum. It reflects an honor-based system, not a collective-discipline machine.
cards.gradeReason: Good cultural distinction baked into the mechanic — needs the lore context to fully land.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: proud individual warrior. Subject: single warrior holding decorative Celtic shield, surrounded by but separate from a crowd. Mood: honorable isolation.

cards.power: Technological Adoption. When an opponent uses a new tactic, copy it immediately and claim you invented it.
cards.lore: The Gauls invented it. The Romans wore it. Medieval knights get the credit. Historiography is just organized theft.
cards.gradeReason: You ARE Roman historiography — copy, rename, take credit. Immediately performable comedy.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: plagiarism satire. Subject: Roman wolf wearing Gallic chainmail, pointing to a patent scroll with his name on it. Mood: smug institutional theft.

cards.power: Ceremonial Distraction. Equip to draw all enemy attacks to this unit, because it looks absolutely fabulous.
cards.lore: From simple caps to spectacular winged parade helmets. The metallurgical sophistication was so high, Roman auxiliary units just wore the local gear.
cards.gradeReason: Great humor — 'absolutely fabulous' lands but the card needs a performer who commits to the bit.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: fashion disaster battlefield illustration. Subject: warrior in spectacular winged parade helmet drawing all eyes and arrows. Mood: dazzling strategic vanity.

cards.power: Resource Denial. Burn your own resource deck. The opponent immediately starves and loses half their hand.
cards.lore: Vercingetorix's doctrine: destroy your own grain to break the Roman supply chain. The hardest part was convincing the tribes to do it.
cards.gradeReason: Solid sacrifice mechanic — lore captures the political tragedy, power stays functional.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: anguished sacrifice. Subject: Gallic leader burning his own grain stores while soldiers watch in horror. Mood: necessary devastation.

cards.power: Mobile Fortress. Turn your discard pile into a defensive wall. It takes three turns to breach.
cards.lore: The moving city of the Helvetii turned into an impromptu fortress at Bibracte, proving that migrating badgers do not go down easily.
cards.gradeReason: Logistical card — discard-pile-wall is clever but the mechanic is dry, no invitation to perform.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: wagon fortress illustration. Subject: circle of wagons locked together, badgers defending from atop. Mood: stubborn defensive improvisation.

cards.power: Exposed Flank. Attack the card on the far edge of the opponent's board for double damage.
cards.lore: The Gauls wrapped around the unsecured Roman flank. The strategic psychology of a whole empire was born in this panic.
cards.gradeReason: Clean historical event card — good flank mechanic but doesn't invite much beyond tactical play.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: battle map satire. Subject: Gallic wolves wrapping around the edges of an orderly Roman formation. Mood: elegant tactical humiliation.

cards.power: Capital Siege. Occupy an opponent's territory. They pay you gold every turn until you leave.
cards.lore: They weren't conquering barbarians stumbling into an empty city. They conducted a seven-month siege and extracted maximum leverage.
cards.gradeReason: You extract rent from Rome and never leave — player immediately inhabits the extortion.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: occupier comfort illustration. Subject: bears lounging in Roman forum, collecting sacks of gold from embarrassed senators. Mood: casual maximum leverage.

cards.power: Absolute Leverage. Change the win conditions of the game while you are currently winning.
cards.lore: Woe to the conquered. Brennus's response when the Romans complained about the scales. The permanent truth of every asymmetric negotiation.
cards.gradeReason: Changing the rules WHILE WINNING — this is the most arrogant move in the deck. You feel it in your bones.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: triumphant negotiation. Subject: bear throwing sword onto scales, watching Roman diplomat's expression collapse. Mood: asymmetric contempt.

cards.power: Pincer Movement. Trap a unit in the space between two of your own to instantly destroy it.
cards.lore: The Romans caught a Gallic army between two consular armies. The last tactical expression of the naked warrior charge in Italy.
cards.gradeReason: Pure tactical mechanic — pincer is clear but invites no persona, no performance.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: tactical trap illustration. Subject: Roman armies closing from both sides on a cornered Gallic warrior. Mood: the end of an era.

cards.power: Narrative Management. Even if you lose the battle, you get to write the score sheet.
cards.lore: The Helvetii nearly broke the legions. Caesar claimed victory, marched them home, and wrote the first chapter of his PR masterpiece.
cards.gradeReason: Great concept — 'write the score sheet' is immediately appealing but needs a moment to explain at table.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: spin doctor illustration. Subject: vulture writing at desk while chaos erupts behind him, annotating a defeat as a victory. Mood: editorial omnipotence.

cards.power: Flank Rescue. Play instantly when you are about to lose. Save your board and score out the attackers.
cards.lore: The Roman regiment that hit the Nervii from the flank just as Caesar was grabbing a shield and looking for a life in the front lines.
cards.gradeReason: Solid rescue card — reactive play is clear but performs for Rome, not the Gallic table energy.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: last-second rescue. Subject: Roman legion wolves charging from the side at the exact moment of collapse. Mood: institutional reliability.

cards.power: Political Extortion. Steal an opponent's card. If they attack you, you rip it.
cards.lore: Caesar attempted to take Dumnorix to Britain as a hostage. Standard Roman operating procedure: hold their kids, take their land.
cards.gradeReason: 'If they attack you, you rip it' — you feel the hostage in your hand. Chilling, immediate, performable.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: cold political illustration. Subject: Roman eagle holding a small card delicately while smiling at the card's owner. Mood: civilized menace.

cards.power: Fatal Sentimentality. Refuse to destroy one of your own resource cards. The opponent captures it and wins the game.
cards.lore: The one town the Gallic council refused to burn. Caesar took it, used its grain, and continued the campaign. Sentimentality is a vulnerability.
cards.gradeReason: Dark lesson card — the irony is perfect but 'Refuse to destroy' is instruction, the invitation is in the name.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: tragic preservation. Subject: Gallic leader clutching a model town to his chest while Caesar watches from the distance. Mood: doomed tenderness.

cards.power: Double Walls. Build a wall facing your opponent, and a wall facing the rest of the room. You can't move, but neither can they.
cards.lore: Fifty kilometers of earthworks. Fighting on two fronts simultaneously. The most terrifying engineering flex in military history.
cards.gradeReason: 'A wall facing the rest of the room' — instantly spatial, immediately physical. Players build it in their imagination.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: paranoid fortress engineering. Subject: soldier building walls in all directions at once, looking panicked. Mood: control that traps everyone.

cards.power: Mass Coordination. Combine the attack power of every single card in your deck for one Turn. If it fails, you lose instantly.
cards.lore: 250,000 warriors from across Gaul, assembled to break the Roman perimeter. They failed by the thinnest of margins.
cards.gradeReason: Everything at once or nothing — highest stakes possible. You feel the weight of 250,000 people.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: desperate surge illustration. Subject: enormous wave of Gallic animals cresting over Roman earthworks, outcome uncertain. Mood: all-or-nothing terror.

cards.power: Absolute Commitment. Exhaust your entire hand to add +1 to a crucial roll.
cards.lore: Caesar personally rode along the line with cavalry to stabilize the collapsing perimeter. The final engagement lasted a day and a night.
cards.gradeReason: Exhausting your entire hand for +1 feels underwhelming against the name's promise of 'Absolute Commitment.'
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: desperate cavalry charge. Subject: commander on horseback riding along a crumbling defensive line at dawn. Mood: exhausted total commitment.

cards.power: Cruel Display. Keep a defeated leader on your board for six turns before discarding it, just to demoralize the opponent.
cards.lore: Caesar kept Vercingetorix in a cell for six years just to parade him in his triumph. The ultimate political communication.
cards.gradeReason: Political theater as pure game mechanic — you are made to watch your defeated hero for six turns.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: public humiliation pageant. Subject: chained stag displayed on a victory float, Roman crowd cheering, Gallic spectators looking away. Mood: political cruelty as performance.

cards.power: Logistics Hack. Store unused resources indefinitely.
cards.lore: Gallic barrel logistics moved the Roman army. The technology survived; the culture that produced it was reclassified as 'barbarians.'
cards.gradeReason: Dry utility card — the lore is the entire joke, the power is just a storage mechanic.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: ironic technology illustration. Subject: Roman soldier proudly patenting a barrel while Gallic inventor watches unnamed. Mood: credit theft.

cards.power: Frictionless Advance. Move your cards twice as fast across the board.
cards.lore: The Celtic metallurgical mastery that allowed chariots and wagons to conquer rough terrain. Rome rode on Gallic rims.
cards.gradeReason: Good lore, dry mechanic — movement speed card doesn't invite performance.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: technology pride illustration. Subject: gleaming iron wheel rim rolling fast while Roman engineers take notes. Mood: unacknowledged excellence.

cards.power: Endless Sustenance. Generate +1 food token every turn forever.
cards.lore: The Gallic invention that fed Europe for a thousand years. Caesar destroyed the druids, but he kept the bread-makers.
cards.gradeReason: Pure sustenance utility — lore is strong but the card is bread, not theater.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: working class dignity illustration. Subject: mouse miller working a rotary mill, Roman legions eating in the background. Mood: essential invisible labor.

cards.power: The Erasure. Remove a faction from the rulebook entirely.
cards.lore: Caesar's response to Ambiorix's trap: the systematic, complete destruction of a tribe, written down with bureaucratic indifference.
cards.gradeReason: Erasing a faction from the rulebook IS genocide as game mechanic. Most disturbing card in the deck. Unforgettable.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: bureaucratic horror. Subject: administrative fox calmly erasing a whole section of a rulebook while a tribe fades behind him. Mood: indifferent extinction.

cards.power: Rule Vandalism. Cross out any printed rule on an opponent's card and write your own.
cards.lore: FrizzleBob notes that the sentence that begins the conquest is written in the language of the conqueror. Time to edit.
cards.gradeReason: Physically crossing out text and writing new rules — pure meta-play embodiment of the FrizzleBob identity.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: editorial chaos. Subject: deranged rabbit with red pen crossing out printed text on a card while cackling. Mood: joyful institutional vandalism.

cards.power: Gutter Attack. Your margin doodles come alive and eat the opponent's resource tokens. If it looks designed or corporate, damage it. The truth lives in the messy, chaotic, unhinged margins.
cards.lore: If it looks designed or corporate, damage it. The truth lives in the messy, chaotic, unhinged margins.
cards.gradeReason: Great concept — power text appears duplicated/merged with lore; needs clean editorial separation.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: doodle uprising. Subject: scribbled margin creatures pouring off the edge of a card and eating corporate symbols. Mood: anarchic analog revenge.

cards.power: Cut & Paste. Physically cut one of your cards in half to double its number of units, halving its health.
cards.lore: The Roman system was a rigid machine. The FrizzleBob system is a pair of scissors and zero respect for institutional boundaries.
cards.gradeReason: Fun concept but 'physically cut your card' is impractical as a mechanic — needs [JOKER] exemption caveat.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: DIY chaos illustration. Subject: rabbit with scissors cutting a card in half gleefully. Mood: creative destruction with consequences.

cards.power: Permanent Haunting. You win the moral victory. The game ends in a draw, but the opponent feels bad about it.
cards.lore: The druids are gone. The cathedral was built. But the water still flows beneath it. Vae victis.
cards.gradeReason: Winning the MORAL VICTORY while drawing — the most haunting way to close a deck. Perfect last card.
cards.artworkPrompt: Style: underground persistence. Subject: spring flowing beneath cathedral stones, water carrying small druidic symbols forward. Mood: quiet eternal undefeated sadness.

verdict: Wine, Woad & Warrior Chiefs is the deck that makes Gallic history something you DO, not something that was done to you. The power mechanics consistently enact the historical irony — Vae Victis changes the rules while you're winning, The Six-Year Wait makes the opponent watch their defeated hero for six full turns, Eburones Annihilation erases a faction from the rulebook entirely. The Epistemic Sabotage finale with FrizzleBob's Red Pen and The Spring Remembers is the best closing sequence in the corpus. Fix the garbled 'Divided into Three Parts' power text before Gumroad, and add a joker caveat to Analog-First DIY Logic. Table-ready: YES.
blurb: Fifty-two cards of Celtic defiance, Roman gaslighting, and naked warriors who make the math not apply to them. For anyone who suspects history is propaganda written by the winners — and wants to play the other side.

coverQA.coverVisual: 5 — stunning full-spread illustration with rabbit in Roman helmet, wild animals, blue-red swirl energy
coverQA.coverTitle: 5 — 'Wine, Woad & Warrior Chiefs' is alliterative, memorable, immediately curious
coverQA.coverVibeMatch: 5 — perfectly captures satirical-educational tone; 'drawn by a deranged rabbit' sets expectations exactly
coverQA.coverOriginality: 4 — strong concept, but rabbit mascot is familiar in corpus; the pose and tagline are the freshest elements
coverQA.coverViral: 5 — highly shareable; subtitle is quotable and the illustration stops thumbs
coverQA.coverNote: This cover does exactly what a cover should do: tells you what the game IS before you open it. The tagline 'History is written by the victors. This deck is drawn by a deranged rabbit.' is the single best deck-summary sentence in the corpus. The BLÖDSINN hedgehog lurking in the corner is a nice in-universe touch.

notes: 14 pages: 1 cover + 13 content pages, 4 cards per page = 52 cards total. No RAF dice boxes visible. Section headers used as page titles throughout, each with satirical subtitle — strong structural rhythm. Deck opens with propaganda mechanics and closes with epistemic sabotage/FrizzleBob meta-cards — excellent narrative arc. 'The Margin Infestation' (card 50) has duplicated/merged power and lore text — same paragraph appears in both fields; needs editorial fix. 'Divided into Three Parts' power text is garbled with 'must not exist in each' — likely draft error needing rewrite. Uncle FrizzleBob appears as a named card character on the final page — bold and correct. KayfaBIZARRO and BLÖDSINN tags visible on multiple pages as in-universe watermarks. PDF dimensions: landscape 745x415pt (standard web ID format). Tech patent section (cards 45-47) is the deck's only dry stretch — three back-to-back utility cards without performative hooks.

urgent: Fix 'Divided into Three Parts' power text — 'Opponent must not exist in each' is unplayable as written; rewrite the mechanic clearly
Fix 'The Margin Infestation' card 50 — power and lore text are identical/merged; needs clean editorial separation
quickWins: Add [JOKER] exemption note to 'Analog-First DIY Logic' — literal scissors instruction needs a safety valve
Consider adding cut-here markers to pages 13-14 which appear to have fewer guides than earlier pages
niceToHave: Tech patent section (cards 45-47) is the deck's only dry stretch — consider one more performative card to break the logistics run
Battle of Bibracte and Battle of the Allia would benefit from a slightly stronger power-line hook
'Nearly ending Caesar's career in an afternoon' (Nervii lore) is strong enough to be a standalone card title

marketingText:
Kayfabizarro: WINE, WOAD & WARRIOR CHIEFS – The Gauls Cross-Examine Their Own Obituary (Free Cut & Play Comic Card Game)

Who told you the Gauls lost? The man who slaughtered them, then wrote the only book that survived.

Here is the problem with Gaul. There is one eyewitness on the record, and he is also the prosecutor, the executioner, and the publisher. Caesar wrote the Commentarii while he was still invoicing the Senate for the war, so every Gaul in the account exists to make the invasion look necessary, even noble. Vae victis, woe to the conquered, who never get to file a rebuttal. This deck is the rebuttal.

Wine, Woad and Warrior Chiefs hands you the other side of the table. Social Story Wrestling: 52 cut-and-play cards where you take a tribe, a tactic, or a piece of Roman gaslighting, perform it out loud, and let the room rule on whether it holds the line or gets quietly written out of the record by the side with the better PR. Woad-painted, outnumbered, and entirely uninterested in the math.

WHAT'S INSIDE?
- The Wine, Woad & Warrior Chiefs Core Deck: 52 High-Res "Print, Cut & Play" Cards, featuring Vae Victis (The Ransom Gold), the day a Gaulish chief dropped his sword onto a scale already weighed against Rome and dared anyone to complain; Eburones Annihilation, an entire people wiped off the map and refiled under "pacified" by the only man counting the bodies; and Dumnorix of the Aedui, who refused the boats, rode off shouting that he was a free man of a free people, and was run down for the crime of meaning it.
- The Freestyle Rules: The complete Anti-Rulebook. No complicated math, just storytelling, dice-driven chaos, and the Winner Writes the Recap rule, where whoever takes the match narrates what happened, and that version becomes the history everyone inherits next round.
- The Propaganda Engine: the deck opens by teaching you how a conquest gets sold and closes by handing you the eraser, FrizzleBob's meta-cards that let you sabotage the official account and rebook the ending from the losing side.

THE "LIVING DECK" PASS (Free Updates)
You are not buying a static PDF. You are enlisting in the KayfaBizarro historical campaign. Every future deck in this cycle, more empires, more screwjobs, more winners caught editing the tape, lands in your library as a free update.

WHY "PAY WHAT YOU WANT"?
The winners already wrote their version and got it printed at public expense. I make these to print the other side. Are you broke? Enter "0" and take it. Cut it, play it, argue with the dead at your own table. Want to support the craft? Every dollar goes straight into the next cards and the next obituary worth contesting.
